mainTopic: Why the Torah writes both "ראשו" and "זקנו" by the shaving of a מצורע, and how רבי אליעזר learns that an עשה pushes aside a לא תעשה
overview: The גמרא finishes explaining why the Torah needs both words, "his head" (ראשו) and "his beard" (זקנו), when it commands a מצורע to shave. If only "his head" were written, it would teach two things. First, it would teach that an עשה overrides a לא תעשה. Second, it would teach that shaving the whole head counts as forbidden rounding (הקפה). But it would not teach that the shaving must be done with a razor (תער), so the Torah adds "his beard." Then the גמרא asks where רבי אליעזר learns the rule of עשה דוחה לא תעשה. It answers that he learns it from ציצית (גדילים). It begins quoting a ברייתא about שעטנז to show this, and the ברייתא continues on the next amud.

steps.title: What "his head" alone would have taught
steps.stepSummary: If the Torah had written only "ראשו," we would have learned two things from it: עשה דוחה לא תעשה, and that rounding the whole head counts as הקפה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the Torah had written only "his head" and not "his beard," I would have said that "his head" teaches two things. First, that a positive מצוה comes and overrides a prohibition. Second, that rounding off the entire head is also called "rounding."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is explaining why both words are needed. It starts by showing what we could learn if only "his head" were written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word "ראשו" tells the מצורע to shave his head, even though there is a prohibition against rounding the corners of the head. So it teaches two things: the עשה of shaving overrides the לאו, and shaving the entire head counts as forbidden הקפה, which is why an override is needed at all. This prepares the next step, which shows what is still missing.

keyTerms.meaning: A positive מצוה, a command to do something
Rounding off the corners of the head, which is forbidden

phrases.english: And if [the Torah] had written "his head"
I would have said: it teaches two things:

phrases.english: that a positive מצוה comes and overrides a prohibition,
and it teaches that rounding the entire head

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי כְּתַב ״רֹאשׁוֹ״ וְלָא כְּתַב ״זְקָנוֹ״, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the explanation from the previous amud of why both ראשו and זקנו are needed.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: Perhaps "ראשו" alone would be enough for everything
steps.terutzMaskana: "ראשו" covers two teachings but not everything, as the next step shows

steps.title: "His beard" teaches shaving with a razor
steps.stepSummary: Even with "ראשו," we still would not know the shaving must be with a תער, so the Torah wrote "זקנו" to teach that.
steps.simpleTranslation: But still, how would we know that he must shave with a razor? For this reason the Torah also wrote "his beard."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out what "his head" cannot teach, which is that a razor is required. It answers that this is why "his beard" is written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The razor requirement comes from the beard. The Torah's prohibition on destroying the beard is about removal with a razor, so connecting the מצורע's shaving to the beard shows he must use a razor. This finishes the answer: each word has its own job.

keyTerms.meaning: And still, there is still a gap
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah or ה׳

steps.whatToRemember: "ראשו" teaches עשה דוחה לא תעשה and that rounding the whole head is הקפה. "זקנו" adds that the shaving is done with a razor.

phrases.english: And still, [that he shaves] with a razor, from where do we know it?
For this reason the Merciful One wrote "his beard."
phrases.notes: Beard shaving that the Torah forbids is done with a razor, so mentioning the beard brings the razor in.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the gap left by step 1 and fills it with "זקנו."
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigns a separate teaching to the second word
steps.terutzMaskana: "זקנו" is needed to teach that a razor is required

steps.title: Where does רבי אליעזר learn that an עשה overrides a לאו?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what source רבי אליעזר uses for the rule of עשה דוחה לא תעשה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי אליעזר, from where does he learn that a positive מצוה comes and overrides a prohibition?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to רבי אליעזר and asks for his source for the rule that an עשה pushes aside a לא תעשה. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The approach we just finished learned this rule from the מצורע verses. The question assumes רבי אליעזר does not learn it from there, so he must have a different source.

keyTerms.meaning: From where does he know it?
A תנא whose opinion is being examined

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָתֵי עֲשֵׂה וְדָחֵי אֶת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה מְנָלֵיהּ?
phrases.english: that a positive מצוה comes and overrides a prohibition, from where does he derive it?

steps.title: He learns it from ציצית
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר learns the rule from "גדילים" (ציצית), and the גמרא begins quoting a ברייתא that starts with the prohibition of שעטנז.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns it from "fringes," as a ברייתא teaches: "You shall not wear diverse kinds [wool and linen together]..."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי אליעזר's source is ציצית. It starts quoting a ברייתא to show how, and the ברייתא continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah puts the ban on שעטנז right next to the מצוה of making גדילים. This hints that the מצוה of ציצית can override the ban on wool and linen together, which is a clear case of an עשה pushing aside a לא תעשה. The rest of the ברייתא will lay this out.

keyTerms.meaning: Wool and linen woven together, forbidden to wear
He learns it, he derives it
As it is taught in a ברייתא

steps.confusionAlert: The quote does not end here. The ברייתא continues on the next amud, so the full proof comes there.

phrases.notes: דברים 22:12, the verse right after the שעטנז ban.

phrases.english: As it is taught in a ברייתא:

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי אליעזר learns עשה דוחה לא תעשה from the מצוה of ציצית placed next to שעטנז, proven through a ברייתא
